newsitem.title: TAIWAN: CPC offloading crude at reopened Taiwan port.
newsitem.headline: CPC offloading crude at reopened Taiwan port.

text.p: State-owned Chinese Petroleum on Thursday resumed crude offloading at its northern Taiwan crude port, hoping to pump 550,000 tonnes of crude from two tankers, officials at its adjacent Taoyuan refinery said.
"Our engineers have reported from the offshore crude port that the offloading process for one tanker has started," refinery official Wang Kao-li told Reuters by telephone.

An official at the company's Taipei headquarters said the tanker Vanadis, which had been stalled at Taoyuan throughout the port's 16-day shutdown, was now pumping its 300,000-tonne cargo and expected to complete the offloading within three days.
"The reopened crude offloading unit only has one of its two undersea pipes fixed, so the Vanadis is discharging at half of the normal speed," the official said.
The second unit remained closed, officials said.

The crude port was first shut down on September 15 due to unspecified pipeline problems, shutting off the flow of crude to the Taoyuan refinery and forcing it to run at just 34 percent of capacity as its crude supplies waned.
Rough seas caused by a series of typhoons have thwarted repairs, keeping the port closed since mid-September with the exception of a brief period on September 25.
The 250,000-tonne Felipe Camarao would begin offloading its cargo once the second unit is repaired or the Vanadis is finished, the headquarters official said.
Refinery officials were meeting late on Thursday afternoon to decide whether to increase production now that the supply of crude has been restored.
No decision had been made, officials said.
Low crude supplies had forced Chinese Petroleum to shut one of the refinery's two 100,000-barrel-per-day distillation or topping units to slow its crude consumption.
The Taoyuan refinery's main product is jet oil, turning out 60,000 tonnes a month at full capacity. It is the principal supplier to Taipei's busy international airport at Taoyuan.
The slowed production forced Chinese Petroleum to increase its purchases of jet oil in the Asian energy market.
Chinese Petroleum has bought two 32,000-tonne shipments of jet fuel since the refinery's cut production and issued another tender on Tuesday for one more shipment.
